subject: Acme - Performance SLO & concurrency follow-up
summary: Post-call follow-up collecting concurrency and latency targets, negotiating Redwood hosted rate limits vs Dedicated capacity and next steps for formal quote/PO.
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Simon Lee <simon.lee@acme.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>, David Kim <david@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 1 Dec 2026 15:12:00 -0800
Subject: Acme - Performance SLO & concurrency follow-up

Hi Simon — great call today, thanks for walking through Acme's realtime assistant use case. Quick recap and a few follow-ups so we can size concurrency/quotas and put together a recommended configuration + quote.

Recap (high level):
- Use case: in-product assistant that streams partial responses while the model continues generating (progressive streaming).
- Target SLOs: 95th percentile latency target for streaming chunks: 250-300ms; end-to-end median generation ~500ms (TBD).
- Peak patterns: short, intense bursts around product events, sustained baseline during business hours.

Info we need from your side (small asks):
1) Peak concurrent requests (parallel streaming connections) at 95th percentile during event-driven bursts.
2) Expected sustained concurrent requests during regular business hours.
3) Average input + output tokens per request (or an example request/sample).
4) Any hard constraints on per-request latency (p95/p99) or time-to-first-byte for streamed responses.

Redwood baseline & options:
- Hosted (fastest to run): default tenant concurrency on our hosted API is conservatively limited; typical scaling supports 50-200 concurrent streaming requests for standard models without dedicated capacity. We can raise quotas for larger customers.
- Dedicated: reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and high concurrency (thousands of parallel requests depending on commit).

Attachments: I attached our Redwood rate-limits summary (redwood-rate-limits.pdf) and a draft mutual action plan (acme-mpa-draft-v1.pdf).

Next steps: if you can send the numbers above, we’ll propose two configurations: (A) Hosted with increased quota and connection-pooling guidance, and (B) Dedicated capacity profile with expected latency and cost. We can then issue a formal quote/PO path.

Thanks — Marissa
Marissa Cole
Account Exec, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com
(415) 555-0142

From: Simon Lee <simon.lee@acme.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: ACME Procurement <procurement@acme.com>
Date: Wed, 2 Dec 2026 09:24:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Acme - Performance SLO & concurrency follow-up

Thanks Marissa — good notes. Below are the initial numbers from our telemetry and engineering estimates:

1) Peak concurrent streaming connections (95th during events): ~500 concurrent streams (these are short-lived bursts lasting ~2-5 minutes).
2) Sustained concurrent during business hours: ~120 concurrent streams.
3) Average tokens: user input ~20 tokens, model output median ~60 tokens; tail to ~250 tokens on complex queries.
4) Latency requirements: we'd like time-to-first-byte for the first streaming chunk <300ms p95; overall p95 end-to-end generation ideally <700ms but can tolerate up to 1s for complex requests.

A couple of follow-up Qs: 
- Does Redwood count concurrent streaming connections the same as standard concurrent requests for rate limit purposes?
- For hosted quota increases, what's a realistic ramp schedule and typical approval: can we get an interim higher quota for a pilot?

CC'ing procurement for visibility — they'll want a ballpark cost sheet before moving to PO.

Simon
Simon Lee
Sr. Eng Manager, Conversational AI
Acme Corp
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: Simon Lee <simon.lee@acme.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>, David Kim <david@redwood.com>
Date: Thu, 3 Dec 2026 11:03:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Acme - Performance SLO & concurrency follow-up

Simon — thanks, that's exactly what we need. Answers inline and recommended next steps below.

Quick answers:
- Concurrency accounting: yes — for hosted rate limits we treat an active streaming connection that consumes tokens as a concurrent request for quota purposes. Each parallel streaming socket counts toward your concurrency allotment while it's active.
- Pilot quota increases: we can provision a time-limited quota bump for pilots (typically 2–4 weeks) while we qualify traffic patterns.

Recommended configurations (based on your numbers):
Option A — Hosted (fast path, lower commitment):
- Pilot quota: bump to 600 concurrent streaming connections for 2 weeks to validate burst behavior.
- Token rate: soft limit set to 3M tokens/minute tenant-wide; adjustable after pilot based on observed token burn.
- Network/clients: use connection pooling and persistent HTTP/2 or keep-alive sockets; enforce a 30s idle timeout before connection recycling.
- Fallback: automated graceful backpressure when concurrency > quota with 429 + Retry-After header; we'll provide client-side guidance for exponential backoff and limited retries.

Option B — Dedicated (recommended if you need predictable p95 during sustained high concurrency):
- Reserved pool sized to target 700+ concurrent streaming requests sustained, with headroom for 1.2x bursts.
- Dedicated autoscaling policy and priority routing to ensure p95 latency targets.
- SLA-backed uptime and latency targets can be added to the contract.

Technical notes attached: redwood-rate-limits.pdf includes the hosted concurrency accounting table, streaming chunking guidance, and recommended client retry settings.

Next steps:
1) We'll provision a hosted pilot quota (600 concurrency) as soon as you sign the pilot MPA; I attached a draft MPA for review.
2) Laura (copied) will prepare a configuration recommendation and an internal pre-sales note with estimated cost delta for the hosted pilot vs Dedicated baseline.
3) If procurement is ready, we'll produce a formal pilot quote and PO path.

If this looks ok I'll start the pilot provisioning process and loop in operations for the quota change.

— Marissa
From: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: David Kim <david@redwood.com>, Simon Lee <simon.lee@acme.com>
Date: Sat, 5 Dec 2026 10:47:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Acme - Performance SLO & concurrency follow-up

Marissa / Simon — adding a few technical callouts from pre-sales/solutions:

- Connection pooling: we recommend HTTP/2 or long-lived HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with a pool size tuned to the client tier. For browsers/clients that can't hold many sockets, use a proxy or connection-multiplexing edge.
- Streaming chunk sizing: aim for ~128–256 token chunks for a good tradeoff between latency and token efficiency. This reduces p95 time-to-first-byte and keeps more efficient batching on the server.
- Batching & KV cache: configure prefix caching for repeated prompts to reduce per-token compute and preserve p95.
- Canary rollout: start with 10% of traffic on pilot quota for 48 hours, then 50% for one business day, then 100% if metrics look good (latency, error rate, token burn).

I'll attach a short runbook in the drive link for the ops team (see related_links). Also, for the hosted pilot we should include a simple aborted-request metric so we can tune client-side timeouts.

— Laura
Principal Solutions Engineer, Redwood
From: Simon Lee <simon.lee@acme.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
Cc: ACME Procurement <procurement@acme.com>
Date: Thu, 10 Dec 2026 09:30:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Acme - Performance SLO & concurrency follow-up

Thanks Marissa / Laura — this all sounds reasonable. We're happy to run the hosted pilot with the 600 concurrency quota for two weeks and follow the canary rollout plan. Procurement, can you review the attached MPA draft and advise on next steps for a pilot PO?

Action items we'll own:
- Share a sample of real request traces and a couple example prompts (tokens) by EOD Friday so you can validate chunk sizes.
- Add a short client-side retry/backoff per Laura's guidance.

Marissa — please go ahead and provision the pilot quota once procurement confirms, and share the formal pilot quote.

Simon
